https://www.dw.com/en/war-in-ukraine-why.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I6e7 An oil tank storage facility on fire in Feodosiya in southeastern Crimea after a Ukrainian attack in October 2024 Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement In an attempt to isolate Crimea from the mainland, the Ukrainian armed forces have intensified their attacks on the peninsula, which was invaded and annexed by Russia in 2014. Ukraine is using long-range drones to attack transports on the M14 highway between the Russian city of Rostov-on-Don and Melitopol in occupied southern Ukraine. It is also targeting Russian shadow fleet ships in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea , as well as energy facilities that supply the Russian military. Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander of the Ukrainian forces for unmanned systems, says 196 Russian ships and more than 100 energy facilities have been hit in the past month alone. His figures cannot be independently verified. Russia appears to be struggling to supply both its military and the civilian population in Crimea. Fuel coupons were issued at the end of May, but ran out after 24 hours, after which gasoline was being traded on the black market. A state of emergency was declared in Crimea, especially Sevastopol, in response to repeated disruption of the electricity and water supply, and of the internet and cellphone networks. What are residents in Crimea experiencing? Nina, a pensioner who lives in a village near Feodosiya, southeastern Crimea, told DW about the difficulties people there are facing: Residents there can't cook because of power cuts, and fuel shortages mean public transport only runs intermittently. Nina's worst fear, though, is not having electricity in winter. Russian-occupied Crimea hit by fuel shortages and power cuts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The longest power cuts have been in the north of Crimea. This is where Ivan lives [name changed]. He tells DW that for some time, people were unable to get hold of fuel with either coupons or cash. The only exceptions, he says, were police officers, state officials, and doctors. For several days, everything collapsed: Cars ran out of fuel and simply came to a stop; people didn't know how they were supposed to get to where they were going. Ivan said that most shops no longer stock perishable goods, because they can't run their fridges and freezers: "There are no milk products, or fish, or meat," he said. "There are only a few shops with electricity generators, but the prices there are much higher than before." Some small, private, volunteer initiatives are trying to help. The blogger Olena Gerasimenko works with companies in Simferopol to bring drinking water to people suffering from power cuts, and to hospitals and kindergartens. In her blog, she reports that people are complaining about the lack of help from the Russian-installed "authorities" in Crimea. On social media, people say that, because of the power cuts and having no means of communication, residents of northern Crimea are sending post by public bus. But the buses aren't running regularly either. What are Ukraine's tactics? Ukraine's efforts to block supply routes both in and to Crimea are directed primarily against the small Russian tankers and tugboats that transport oil to larger ships and fuel to the Crimean mainland. Parallel to this, it is also destroying transformer substations. But Commander Brovdi says Ukraine is deliberately sparing the Kerch Bridge , which spans the Kerch Strait, connecting the peninsula with the Russian region of Krasnodar. In a recent interview with the Irish journalist Caolan Robertson , Brovdi said the road and rail bridge should be maintained as a corridor for people to escape from Crimea. The aim is not to destroy it, Brovdi says, but to cut off Russian troops from supplies and reinforcements. "We want to make it impossible for the Russian military machine to remain and continue to operate there." Satellite photo of the Henichesk Bridge, damaged by Ukrainian attacks, and a new, alternative bridge connecting Russian-occupied southern Ukraine to northern Crimea Image: Vantor/REUTERS The military expert Ivan Kyrychevskyi serves in a Ukrainian drone unit. Speaking to DW he emphasized how important the air attacks on Crimea are for the frontline on the ground. "To stop the Russians getting anywhere near Zaporizhzhia , they have to put pressure on their lines of communication in the occupied south of Ukraine. This applies above all to Crimea. The blockade of shipping traffic in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea essentially has the same objective," says Kyrychevskyi. "For far too long, Crimea has served the Russians as a tranquil harbor and unsinkable aircraft carrier from which to carry out their offensives in southern Ukraine." Pavlo Narozhnyi, a Ukrainian military expert and founder of the charitable organization Reactive Post, describes Crimea as a massive military base. Russian troops in the regions of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia are heavily dependent on it. Narozhnyi says that for a long time Russian logistics primarily ran through the peninsula, but this supply source is now being cut off on two sides: On land by attacks on the M14 highway, and at sea by attacks on transport vessels near the Crimea Bridge. "This way we are not isolating only Crimea but also the Russian troops in the south of Ukraine," Narozhnyi told DW. His organization supplies life-saving equipment to Ukrainian artillery divisions on the frontline. Situation 'no worse' than in Ukrainian cities3 Narozhnyi explains that, at present, up to three million people in Crimea depend on Russia for their supplies. "A thermal power station that provided up to 60% of Crimea's entire electricity supply has been destroyed. The supply of oil products has been interrupted. The population is already experiencing problems, even with everyday things." The military expert also warned that these problems will get even worse in the fall, when the weather turns colder and people want to heat their homes. "Putin will then have to deal not only with military problems, but also the problems of the population," Narozhnyi says. People use flashlights to navigate a dark street during a power outage in Yevpatoriya, Crimea, in July 2026. Image: Alexey Pavlishak/REUTERS According to Sidharth Kaushal of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in London, attacks on power stations do not automatically contravene international law, particularly if the facilities have military significance and the attacks comply with the rule of proportionality. Ukrainian experts confirm that the targeted facilities primarily supply electricity for military facilities. Kaushal told DW that he assumed a large-scale blockade strategy by Ukraine could ultimately compel Moscow to negotiate a ceasefire. Commander Brovdi is asking people to be patient. "I apologize to the residents of Crimea, the Ukrainians, for the current difficulties. They are experiencing restrictions of advantages they have enjoyed all their lives – the supply of energy, water, and communications. But they are in a situation no worse than that of people in Kharkiv, Dnipro, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Nikopol, Kherson, and hundreds of other cities that are targeted on a daily basis." This article was originally written in Ukrainian. https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian Carers About 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers More than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK says Patrick Butler Social policy editor Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google About 1,500 Britons a day are quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, as they try to balance their vulnerable relatives’ growing care needs with declining access to state-funded social care services. Research estimates that more than a million people have left the workplace to look after ageing, ill and disabled loved ones in the past two years, highlighting the social challenges caused by UK’s rapidly changing demographic profile. Unpaid caring is now a “widespread social and economic reality” for UK households, it says, with one in five employees – equivalent to 6.7 million people – facing career and financial sacrifices as they juggle paid work and care for family or friends. Over a fifth of those surveyed (22%) had reduced their job hours to juggle work and care, with over a third (34%) working less than eight hours a week. Around one in 10 carers said they had turned down promotions or taken on lower-paid roles to stay in work. Emily Holzhausen, the director of policy at Carers UK, said: “These figures represent real people who have had to make difficult decisions about their careers, their financial security and their futures due to the pressures of balancing work and care.” Carers UK, which published the report, called on government to strengthen employment rights for unpaid carers, including introducing a statutory entitlement to 10 days’ annual paid carer’s leave for employees. It urged Louise Casey’s independent review of adult social care , expected to report in the next few months, to recommend policy changes putting carers at the centre of a reformed system, by making it easier for carers to combine work and unpaid care. Midwife Jacqui Hylton, aged 58, gave up her 30-year NHS career to become a full-time carer two years ago when her then 86-year-old mother Winnie’s health took a serious turn for the worse. Hylton moved from Hertfordshire to Leeds to live with Winnie and become her full-time carer. But she is frustrated that her professional skills are going to waste when the NHS faces a midwife shortage. Caring will make it harder for her to return to midwifery as she is unable to work the required number of hours a year to maintain her professional accreditation. Enhanced respite allowance would potentially enable her to keep her hand in at work. “I don’t regret caring for my mum. But financially I’m worse off, my pension will be less than it should have been. It’s lonely at times and its extremely hard work – harder than working in the NHS,” she said. The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions. Around one in five (20%) of UK adults, equivalent to 11 million people, report unpaid care duties. As well as affecting carers’ finances, careers and wellbeing, the report estimates the doubling in the number of people quitting paid work to care over the past seven years comes at an annual £37bn economic cost to the UK. A government spokesperson said: “Unpaid carers make an extraordinary contribution to families, our communities and the economy, and I would like to personally thank Carers UK for their invaluable work in supporting unpaid carers and championing the issues they face every day. “We want to ensure there are good jobs for carers who want to work alongside managing their caring responsibilities. This is why we are exploring how best to support unpaid carers through our review of employment rights.” Explore more on these topics Carers news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.dw.com/en/trump-putin-and-xi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OWQI What's in it for China if it mediates between Russia and the US? Image: Kristina Solovyova/Sputnik/REUTERS Advertisement The administration of US President Donald Trump has stepped up diplomatic efforts this autumn to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine . Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv and its European partners while seeking to draw Moscow back to the negotiating table through a series of concessions, including a deal involving Russian diesel exports to the US and the temporary easing of some sanctions. Yet the Kremlin appears in no hurry to resume meaningful peace talks. Moscow is ready to hold negotiations with Ukraine at a technical level next month, the Kremlin said after the meeting between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on November 21. Putin agreed to resume the peace talks mediated by Washington after November 10, his aide Yury Ushakov said after the meeting. He added that the next round of negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and would focus on "building the security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the war." US special envoy Steve Witkoff at and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during a meeting in St. Petersburg on October 21 Image: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/REUTERS According to his aide, Putin also shared some thoughts with Witkoff on the possible trilateral summit involving US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ushakov pointed out that Beijing is already preparing the meeting. Trilateral summit in China without Ukraine Moscow proposed to hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen, China, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week. According to WSJ sources, Putin hopes to reach an agreement with Trump and Xi on ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Russia. Moscow's proposal for the three-way summit involving Russia, the United States and China — but excluding Ukraine and the European Union — offers a glimpse of the negotiating format the Kremlin would prefer. Russia insists that Ukraine must be prepared to make territorial concessions before negotiations can move forward. Putin has also repeatedly stressed that he is willing to negotiate only if Russian interests are taken into account. According to the WSJ, Putin views the proposed gathering in Shenzhen as a potential new Yalta Conference , referring to the 1945 meeting of the leaders of the United States, Great Britain and the Soviet Union to discuss the defeat of Nazi Germany and the postwar order in Europe. The newspaper reported that Chinese officials had indicated through diplomatic channels that Beijing would not object to the three-way format if Trump agreed to participate. Trump, whose relations with Kyiv have deteriorated significantly in recent weeks, has also expressed openness to such talks. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pointed out during his visit in Oslo on October 20 that talks concerning the future of his country will be acceptable only if Ukraine gets a seat at the negotiating table. What does China stand to gain from the talks? Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin who specializes in China-Russia relations, is not surprised by the Kremlin's proposal. He told DW that Moscow wants to feel respected by Washington and treated as a major international power. The previous US administration was unwilling to discuss questions affecting Ukraine's sovereignty with Russia without Kyiv's participation. Now, Umarov said, the Kremlin believes such negotiations may have become possible. Moscow apparently hopes that any agreement reached at the proposed meeting would prompt the White House to pressure Ukraine and the EU into accepting its terms. But what role would China actually play? Umarov believes Beijing would participate largely as a symbolic partner, rather than as an active mediator responsible for the outcome. "Beijing has no intention of taking responsibility for Ukraine's future," he said. China's leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump agreed to hold a trilateral summit with Russia in Shenzhen Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance Simply attending the summit would not impose any additional obligations on China. "It is hardly surprising that the Kremlin insists on this format," Umarov explained. "Russia wants to demonstrate that it is on an equal footing not only with the United States, but also with China. Yet, objectively speaking, Moscow is not the senior partner in that relationship." Umarov believes China has little direct interest in such negotiations. Even if the leaders issued a joint statement, Beijing would seek language that was as vague and noncommittal as possible, he said. That would allow China to present almost any subsequent development in the war as consistent with the understanding reached at the summit. For Umarov, such flexibility would be essential to Beijing's participation. However, Yurii Poita, a senior associate researcher at the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), offers a different assessment. He believes China and Russia have overlapping strategic interests, particularly in their efforts to promote an alternative security architecture across Eurasia. Both countries, he argues, would benefit from a reduction in Western military presence in Europe and Asia and from a weakening of NATO's influence. "If Russia and China manage to convince the United States to reduce its military presence in Europe and military assistance to Ukraine, Russia would gain additional advantages on the battlefield," Poita told DW. He added that such a development would further undermine the EU's confidence in the United States as a NATO ally. Poita believes Moscow and Beijing would seek precisely these outcomes in any negotiations with Washington. Is Putin's political survival crucial for China? Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, also doubts that Beijing is preparing to take a more active diplomatic role in ending the war. Speaking to DW, Kimmage said China may see the conflict as destabilizing and would prefer to maintain trade relations with Ukraine and other countries in the region. But he believes another priority outweighs those concerns. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin," he said. President Zelenskyy said deciding on Ukraine's future without Ukraine was unacceptable Image: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/picture alliance According to Kimmage, Russia provides China with several geopolitical advantages, including low-cost energy and a foreign policy partner that rarely stands in Beijing's way. He believes China will continue indirectly supporting Russia's military efforts to prevent a Russian defeat. An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said, but ensuring Putin does not lose is crucial. For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so. Does excluding Europe reveal the EU's weakness? Neither Ukraine nor the European Union would be part of the proposed talks in China. Kateryna Krasina, a junior researcher at the Kyiv-based New Geopolitics Network, believes their exclusion could reveal how Beijing actually views their international influence. In her assessment, China's approach suggests that it does not regard Ukraine as an independent player in the negotiations and considers Europe relatively weak. Kimmage, however, argues that excluding Europe from the summit would not necessarily diminish its influence over the course of the negotiations. He acknowledged that European governments may have little power to prevent a meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi. But he pointed to European efforts surrounding the 2025 Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, which he believes helped prevent outcomes that would have been unfavorable to Europe. Kimmage said Europe's influence has grown through financial assistance to Ukraine and extensive defense industry cooperation, particularly involving Germany and other European countries. He argued that European support has played an important role in Ukraine's ability to resist Russian advances. "And that support equals leverage," Kimmage said. He believes Russia, China and the United States may all be interested in portraying Europe as a secondary power, but that such a portrayal would overlook Europe's actual influence. "The optics and the reality are not quite the same," he said, drawing a distinction between the appearance of great-power diplomacy resembling the Yalta Conference and Europe's role in supporting Ukraine. Umarov offers another perspective. He believes that any diplomatic agreement between the US, Russia and China would face the reality on the ground. "China understands that whatever the outcome of negotiations with the United States and Russia, the reality on the ground will be very different and will depend above all on Ukraine," he said. "Whether the Kremlin likes it or not, Ukraine has agency of its own. Neither the United States nor Western countries can fully determine what happens on the battlefield through diplomatic pressure alone." This article was originally published in Russian. https://www.dw.com/en/poland-protesters-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OtEg Prefer DW on Google Donald Tusk's center-left governing alliance had vowed to reverse controversial PiS judicial reforms Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP Advertisement Protesters gathered outside Poland's Constitutional Court on Friday night, with authorities sending police to the scene to secure the court's grounds. It all comes after a statement appeared on the top court's website saying President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy had been suspended for one month. Fellow judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska will lead the institution during this period. According to Warsaw police, officers responded to one judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff. Tusk vows to 'restore rule of law' Swieczkowski is one of a slew of politically aligned judges who were appointed by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk backed the move in a post on X. "Restoring the rule of law is our duty," Tusk said. "After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added. Officers responded to a judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP When Tusk's center-left alliance took over after the 2023 parliamentary election, the group announced it would reverse controversial PiS government reforms in the judiciary. President cancels trip abroad Right-wing Polish President Karol Nawrocki reacted to the situation by canceling a planned trip to Senegal. "At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland," Nawrocki said. Upon returning to Poland, he entered the Constitutional Court, making his way through the police barricade, his chief of staff said early on Saturday. "President Karol Nawrocki, accompanied by the First President of the Supreme Court, Zbigniew Kapinski, entered the Constitutional Tribunal building," Pawel Szefernaker wrote on X. In recent months, Nawrocki had refused to swear in five top court judges nominated by parliament. When these judges instead took their oath before parliament, Swieczkowski had denied them access to the building.
